Background · the cloud

A shared page everyone sees at once

"The cloud" just means computers in data centres storing data and running services for you, through the internet.

A realtime database is like a shared Google Doc: you edit here, your classmate sees it there — instantly. So an app can set the car's mission while the car is driving, with no direct connection at all.

Today  app writes the mission → database syncs → car reads it, live.

Background · Firebase

Google's toolbox for connected apps

What we use

Realtime Database

A NoSQL database stored as one JSON tree — syncs to every connected device the instant anything changes.

Also in the box

Authentication

Sign-in accounts so only the right people and devices can read your data.

Why it's easy

Serverless

Google runs the servers. No setup, no maintenance — you just use it.

Why it's fine

Free tier

Small projects like ours cost nothing. Cross-platform, too.

Background · JSON

Data as a tree of labels

JSON is the internet's standard way to write data — like an ID card made of labelled lines:

  • Curly braces { } hold an object
  • Each line is a "key": value pair
  • Values: text, numbers, true/false, or nested objects

Firebase stores your whole database as one JSON tree — you'll import one today.

{ "name": "Smart Car", "task_id": 7, "is_started": false, "time_remain": 100, "start_point": "A", "end_point": "F" }

Background · RFID

How RFID works

RFID = radio-frequency identification. A reader sends radio waves; a nearby tag answers with its stored ID.

A passive tag has no battery at all — the reader's radio field briefly powers it up, and it transmits back. You already own this technology:

  • The Octopus card in your pocket
  • Library book tags
  • School and office access cards

In the final project

Tags on the road, reader under the car

RFID tags are placed along the track. As the car drives over one, the reader scans it — and the car knows exactly where it is. Like tapping in at an MTR gate.

Read  one tag = one unique ID string, like c3a75214.

Prelab · five steps, no car needed

Build your Firebase

1 · Libraries 2 · Project 3 · Database 4 · API key 5 · User

At the end you'll hold three "ID papers" your code needs — keep them safe.

Prelab · Step 1

Two libraries, right versions

Library 01

FirebaseClient ≥ 2.2

Talks to Firebase: login, read, write, stream.

Library 02

ArduinoJson ≥ 7.4

Packs and unpacks JSON — the database's language.

  • In the IDE: Sketch → Include Library → Manage Libraries…
  • Search each name, pick the version, click Install

Prelab · Step 2

Create the project

  • Visit firebase.google.com, sign in with your Google account
  • Click Get Started → Add Project, give it a name
  • You may skip Google Gemini and Google Analytics — Continue
  • Under Build, enable Authentication and Realtime Database

They appear under Project shortcuts once enabled.

Prelab · Step 3

Turn on the Realtime Database

Key 1 of 3  your Database URL — you'll paste it into the code at TODO 1.

Prelab · Step 4

Collect the project key

Click the gear icon next to Project Overview → Project settings → copy the Web API Key.

Not there? Visit console.cloud.google.com/apis → Credentials tab → Show key.

Key 2 of 3  your Web API Key — also TODO 1.

Prelab · Step 5

Set up authentication

  • Authentication → Get started
  • Sign-in method: enable Email/Password
  • Users tab → Add user — email + a simple password you'll remember: it goes into your Arduino code!
  • Firebase shows your User UID — save it
  • Also enable Anonymous sign-in — convenient for the car

Checkpoint 00 · Prelab gate

You now hold three keys.

Key 01

Web API Key

Project settings → the project's master key.

Key 02

Database URL

The internet address of your realtime database.

Key 03

User UID

Your account's random ID — your data lives under it.

Paste all three into a note file — you'll type them into the sketch today

Lab tasks · ESP32 ⇄ Firebase

Reading and writing Firebase

Task 1 · read Task 2 · RFID + write Serial monitor proof

First the car downloads its mission. Then it learns where it is — and tells on itself, live.

Lab · Task 1

Import the mission file

  • Open sample.json, replace <YOUR_UID> with your real UID
  • In the database console, click ⋮ → Import JSON, upload the file
  • Watch the tree appear — start point, end point, task ID, exam status

Why UIDs?  each student's data lives under their own UID — nobody overwrites anybody.

Lab · Task 1

The three TODOs

// TODO 1 — your credentials #define API_KEY "" // ← Web API Key #define DATABASE_URL "" // ← Database URL // TODO 2 — your identity String UID = ""; // ← User UID // TODO 3 — enable the read task xTaskCreatePinnedToCore(firebaseReadTask, "Firebase.Read.Task", 8192, NULL, 2, &firebaseReadTaskHandle, 1); // FreeRTOS, from Lab 5!

Flash it — the Serial Monitor prints the exam state. Now change time_remain to 100 in the web console… the car sees it within seconds. That's realtime sync.

Lab · Task 2

Reading RFID, writing to Firebase

At TODO 3, swap the read task for the Firebase Write Task and the RFID Reader Task:

xTaskCreatePinnedToCore(firebaseWriteTask, …); xTaskCreatePinnedToCore(RFIDTagReaderTask, …);
  • Place a tag under the reader at the bottom of the car
  • Serial prints: RFID Tag: c3a75214
  • Check the console — the car uploaded it by itself

The big picture

The complete data loop

App / website→ Firebase→ Car reads mission→ Car scans RFID→ Location → Firebase→ Everyone sees

Sense (Labs 2) → decide (Lab 5) → connect (today). This exact loop — mission down, location up — is what runs in the final project.
